title: Jeremiah 10:11 and Genesis 31:47

objectives.can: Read the one Aramaic verse of Jeremiah and the Aramaic place-name in Genesis, and say why they are there.

explanation.summary: Besides Daniel and Ezra, the Bible has two more Aramaic passages, and both are tiny. Jeremiah 10:11 is one verse set among Hebrew verses, and Genesis 31:47 contains two Aramaic words, a name that Laban gives to a heap of stones. They show that a book is not 'in Aramaic' or 'in Hebrew': a passage is.

sections.heading: Passages, not books
body: It is natural to say that Daniel is half in Aramaic. It is more exact to say that two passages of Daniel are in Aramaic and the rest is Hebrew. The library follows this: it keeps the Aramaic of Daniel and of Ezra as separate editions, and the same is true of the fifteen words of Jeremiah and the two of Genesis. Each is a small edition of its own, with its own English beside it.

So when a text switches language, a reader should ask where the switch begins and ends, and what is being quoted. In Daniel the switch comes when the Chaldeans speak to the king. In Ezra the Aramaic is that of letters and decrees. In Jeremiah and Genesis the Aramaic is quoted speech.

sections.heading: Jeremiah 10:11: a sentence for the nations
body: The verse stands between Hebrew verses that speak of idols. It opens with an instruction: כִּדְנָה תֵּאמְרוּן לְהוֹם, 'thus you shall say to them'. The adverb כִּדְנָה is the demonstrative דְּנָה with the prefix כִּ, 'like this', 'thus'. תֵּאמְרוּן is a Peal imperfect, second person masculine plural, and the instruction is given to a plural audience. The suffix of לְהוֹם is third person masculine plural. In Daniel you saw this ending as -הוֹן (לְהוֹן, 2:35) and in Ezra as -הֹם (לְהֹם, 5:3); here it is -הוֹם. The three spellings are one suffix, 'them'.

What the audience is to say follows: אֱלָהַיָּא דִּי שְׁמַיָּא וְאַרְקָא לָא עֲבַדוּ יֵאבַדוּ מֵאַרְעָא וּמִן תְּחוֹת שְׁמַיָּא אֵלֶּה. The sentence begins with the determined plural אֱלָהַיָּא, 'the gods'. Then comes a relative clause introduced by דִּי: שְׁמַיָּא וְאַרְקָא לָא עֲבַדוּ, 'who did not make the heavens and the earth'. In it the objects come first, the negative לָא stands before the verb, and the verb is last, a Peal perfect, third person plural. The main verb יֵאבַדוּ, 'they shall perish', is a Peal imperfect, third person plural; it repeats the subject 'the gods' by the demonstrative אֵלֶּה, 'these', at the very end. The place of perishing is given with two prepositional phrases, מֵאַרְעָא, 'from the earth', and וּמִן תְּחוֹת שְׁמַיָּא, 'and from under the heavens'.

The verse has two forms of the word for 'earth': וְאַרְקָא in the relative clause and מֵאַרְעָא after 'from'. Both are determined feminine singular nouns, and they have the same meaning. The form with ק is the older shape of the word, the one that corresponds to the Hebrew letter צ; the form with ע, which is the usual one in Daniel and Ezra, is the later development. The lexica list the first as the form of this verse. Whether the writer chose both forms for a reason or took them from different sources cannot be told from the verse itself.

sections.heading: Why is this verse in Aramaic?
body: The text does not say. One common view is that the verse is a sentence for the nations, spoken in a language they would understand, and that it has been placed in the middle of a Hebrew passage as a quotation. Other views have been put forward, and the question is open. What the grammar does show is that the Aramaic here is the same language as that of Daniel and Ezra, with a few small differences, such as the form of 'these', אֵלֶּה, which is the Hebrew-like form where Daniel has the usual Aramaic אִלֵּין (2:40).

sections.heading: Genesis 31:47: a name for a heap
body: In Genesis 31 Laban and Jacob set up a heap of stones as a witness between them. The Hebrew verse then says that Laban called it by one name and Jacob by another. The first name is Aramaic and has two words: יְגַר שָׂהֲדוּתָא. In the analysis the first is a noun with the sense 'heap' and the second 'testimony'; together, as the edition's English puts it, they make up the name Jegar-sahadutha. The second word has the ending -ָא, the determined state that you know from Daniel. Names like this are a kind of quoted Aramaic: they record the speech of Laban.

Jacob's name for the same heap is Hebrew: גַּלְעֵד. The Hebrew name is outside the Aramaic edition and is given here only to show the contrast; it belongs to the Hebrew text of Genesis. The verse tells the reader that the two men used different languages for the same thing, and the surrounding verses of Genesis give the meaning in Hebrew. There is little here to parse, but the pair is a clear example of how Aramaic enters a Hebrew narrative.

misunderstandings: Saying that Jeremiah, or Genesis, is partly written in Aramaic as if it were a mixed book. They are Hebrew books that quote one Aramaic verse and two Aramaic words.
Treating the different forms לְהוֹן, לְהֹם and לְהוֹם as three different words. They are spellings of one suffix.
Reading וְאַרְקָא and מֵאַרְעָא as two different words with different meanings. They are two forms of the word for 'earth'.
Assuming the grammar can tell us why the Aramaic is there. It can describe what the Aramaic says and how it is built; the reason is a question of interpretation.

deeper.heading: Sound correspondences in the word for 'earth'
body: The Hebrew letter צ corresponds in some words to Aramaic ק and in others to ע. The word for 'earth' is the standard example: the older Aramaic form has ק, the later has ע. In Jeremiah 10:11 both forms stand in one verse. Earlier lessons on the sound correspondences between Hebrew and Aramaic show other examples.

reading.why: The one Aramaic verse of Jeremiah: a sentence of fifteen words with the instruction to speak, a relative clause with the verb last, a plural subject picked up again at the end, and two forms of the word for 'earth'. Genesis 31:47 is read beside it in the examples.
